lead: Unit 3 is where AC stops being mysterious and becomes bookkeeping with complex numbers. By the end you can take any sinusoid, write it as a phasor, find the impedance it sees, solve the circuit with the methods of Units 1 and 2, and state the current, the phase angle, the power and the power factor — single-phase or three-phase, pure sine or distorted.
about: This unit turns the AC circuit into arithmetic on complex numbers, and then into a power bill. Chapter 3.1 fixes the vocabulary: peak, average, RMS, form factor. Chapter 3.2 replaces a sinusoid by a phasor, and 3.3 turns the ratio of phasor voltage to phasor current into impedance. Chapter 3.4 uses those impedances inside mesh, nodal and theorem-based analysis of RL, RC and RLC circuits. Chapter 3.5 reads real, reactive and apparent power out of the same phasors and defines power factor. Chapter 3.6 scales the picture to three phases, balanced and unbalanced, and 3.7 measures three-phase power with two wattmeters. Chapter 3.8, taught at only a few universities, carries RMS and power over to non-sinusoidal waves through Fourier series and THD.

chapters.idea: A sinusoid is fully fixed by its peak, its frequency and its phase, and its heating effect is the RMS value — for a pure sine, peak divided by √2.
chapters.depth: Amplitude (peak) Vm in volts, angular frequency ω = 2πf in rad/s, phase angle φ in degrees or radians, period T = 1/f. Lead and lag between two sinusoids. Average value over a half cycle = 2Vm/π = 0.637 Vm; over a full cycle a pure sine averages zero, so state which average you mean. RMS (effective) value as the square root of the mean of the square; for a sine Vrms = Vm/√2 = 0.707 Vm. Derive that once with a short integral, then quote results for square, triangular and half-wave rectified waves. Form factor = RMS/average = 1.11 for a sine; peak (crest) factor = Vm/Vrms = 1.414. Some syllabi say effective value for RMS and shape factor for form factor.

figure.aria: One half cycle of a sine wave drawn with a horizontal line at 0.637 marking the half-cycle average and a higher line at 0.707 marking the RMS value.

chapters.example: A heater is fed by v(t) = 325 sin(314t) V. Find the peak value, the RMS value, the average over a half cycle, the form factor and the frequency. Peak Vm = 325 V. RMS = 325/√2 = 229.8 V, which is the 230 V a meter would show. ω = 314 rad/s so f = 314/(2π) = 50 Hz. Half-cycle average = 2 × 325/π = 206.9 V. Form factor = 229.8/206.9 = 1.11; peak factor = 325/229.8 = 1.414.
chapters.trap: Using the peak value where RMS belongs (power, meter readings, impedance current), and quoting zero as the average of a sine when the question means the half-cycle average.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the V-I relation of R, L and C; school trigonometry and the idea of an average taken by an integral.
chapters.leave: Phasor notation to 3.2, power formulas to 3.5, RMS of distorted waves to 3.8.

chapters.idea: At one fixed frequency every sinusoid is just a complex number — a vector frozen at t = 0 — so adding sinusoids becomes adding vectors.
chapters.depth: The rotating phasor and Euler's relation, with the phasor keeping only magnitude and phase. RMS phasor versus peak phasor: pick one and keep it. Sine reference versus cosine reference, which shifts every angle by 90°; say which convention the local textbook uses. The operator j as a 90° rotation, and differentiation as multiplication by jω. Adding and subtracting phasors by real and imaginary parts, and converting between rectangular and polar form. Phasor diagrams: take current as the reference for a series circuit, voltage as the reference for a parallel circuit; show lead and lag from the sign of φv − φi. Some syllabi call this the j-notation or complex representation. Keep complex algebra to a two-line refresher box.

figure.aria: Two phasors drawn tip to tail, 20 V at 0 degrees and then 15 V at 60 degrees, with the dashed resultant from the origin at 30.4 V and 25.3 degrees.

chapters.example: Two series voltages v1 = 20 sin(314t) V and v2 = 15 sin(314t + 60°) V. Find the total voltage. Write phasors on the sine reference: V1 = 20∠0°, V2 = 15∠60° = 7.5 + j12.99. Sum = (20 + 7.5) + j12.99 = 27.5 + j12.99, magnitude √(756.25 + 168.75) = 30.4 V, angle tan⁻¹(12.99/27.5) = 25.3°. So v(t) = 30.4 sin(314t + 25.3°) V.
chapters.trap: Changing from a sine to a cosine reference midway and losing the 90° shift, and adding a peak value to an RMS value in the same sum.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for amplitude, ω and phase, and Unit 1 for the element V-I relations.
chapters.leave: Impedance and admittance to 3.3; resonance phasor diagrams to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Impedance Z = V/I is resistance that also remembers the phase shift, and it combines in series and parallel exactly like resistance as long as you keep the j.
chapters.depth: Z_R = R, Z_L = jωL, Z_C = 1/(jωC) = −j/(ωC), all in ohms. Reactance X in ohms, impedance Z = R + jX, magnitude |Z| = √(R² + X²) and angle θ = tan⁻¹(X/R). Admittance Y = 1/Z = G + jB in siemens, with G the conductance and B the susceptance; some books write Y in mho. Series and parallel combination with complex numbers, voltage and current division, and the reciprocal of a complex number taken by multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate. Frequency behaviour: |Z_L| rises with ω, |Z_C| falls. Note that these are the same driving-point immittances that Unit 6 formalises for two-ports.

figure.aria: One sinusoid source fanning out to three element types, each labelled with its impedance expression and its phase angle: resistor 0 degrees, inductor plus 90, capacitor minus 90.

chapters.example: A coil of resistance 8 Ω and inductance 0.02 H is in series with a 100 µF capacitor across 230 V, 50 Hz. Find the impedance, the current and the voltage across the coil. ω = 314.16 rad/s, X_L = 314.16 × 0.02 = 6.28 Ω, X_C = 1/(314.16 × 100 × 10⁻⁶) = 31.83 Ω, so X = 6.28 − 31.83 = −25.55 Ω. Z = 8 − j25.55 Ω, |Z| = 26.77 Ω, θ = −72.6°, so the current leads. I = 230/26.77 = 8.59 A. The coil alone is 8 + j6.28 Ω, |Z_coil| = 10.17 Ω, so V_coil = 8.59 × 10.17 = 87.4 V.
chapters.trap: Giving X_C the wrong sign, and adding resistance to reactance as plain numbers — 8 + j6 is 10 Ω at 36.9°, not 14 Ω.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 for phasors and the j operator.
chapters.leave: The frequency where X_L and X_C cancel (resonance) to Unit 4; two-port Z and Y parameter matrices to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Once each element is written as an impedance, the whole DC toolkit — mesh, nodal, Thevenin, superposition — works unchanged on complex numbers, and the answer is the steady-state response.
chapters.depth: The four steps: source to phasor, elements to Z, solve with mesh or nodal analysis or a network theorem, convert back to a time function. Work series RL, series RC, series RLC, and one parallel or series-parallel case. In a series RLC circuit I = V/Z and the sign of the angle tells you lead or lag; V_L and V_C can each exceed the source voltage while their phasor difference stays small. Treat a practical coil as one impedance R + jX_L. Keep magnitudes as RMS phasors so they read like meter readings. State that the Laplace route of Unit 5 gives the same steady state as its final value, so both roads agree.

figure.aria: A four-step pipeline from a sine source, through impedances and mesh or nodal solution, to a complex current, and finally back to a time-domain expression.

chapters.example: A series RLC circuit with R = 40 Ω, L = 0.15 H and C = 50 µF is connected to v(t) = 230√2 sin(314.16t) V. Find i(t) and the three element voltages. X_L = 47.12 Ω, X_C = 63.66 Ω, X = −16.54 Ω. Z = 40 − j16.54 Ω, |Z| = 43.28 Ω, θ = −22.5°. RMS current = 230/43.28 = 5.31 A, so i(t) = 7.51 sin(314.16t + 22.5°) A. V_R = 212.6 V, V_L = 250.4 V, V_C = 338.3 V, and √(212.6² + (250.4 − 338.3)²) = 230 V, matching the source.
chapters.trap: Stopping at the complex answer without writing the time function and its phase, and subtracting V_L from V_C as if the two were in phase.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 and 3.3, plus Unit 2 for mesh, nodal, superposition and Thevenin.
chapters.leave: Transients, time constants and Laplace to Unit 5; frequency response, Q and bandwidth to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: AC power has a real part that does useful work and a reactive part that swings back to the source; the two together form the complex power S = P + jQ.
chapters.depth: Instantaneous power p(t) = v·i, its double-frequency term, and the average P = Vrms Irms cos φ in watts. Reactive power Q = Vrms Irms sin φ in VAR (volt-ampere reactive), positive for an inductive lagging load and negative for a capacitive leading load. Apparent power S = Vrms Irms in VA, and complex power S = V I* with I* the conjugate current. Power factor = cos φ = P/S, labelled lagging or leading. The power triangle, and the fact that P and Q add across branches while apparent powers do not. Power-factor correction by a parallel capacitor, and why a low power factor costs an industry more on its bill. Keep the tariff discussion general — no invented tariff numbers.

figure.aria: Instantaneous power for a current lagging by 60 degrees: it swings at twice the supply frequency, dips below zero for part of every cycle, and averages 0.25 times peak volts times peak amps.

chapters.example: A 230 V, 50 Hz supply feeds a motor taking 10 A at 0.8 power factor lagging. Find P, Q and S, and the capacitor needed to raise the power factor to 0.95. S = 230 × 10 = 2300 VA. P = 2300 × 0.8 = 1840 W. φ₁ = 36.87°, Q₁ = 2300 × 0.6 = 1380 VAR. At 0.95, φ₂ = 18.2°, Q₂ = 1840 × tan 18.2° = 605 VAR. The capacitor must supply Q_C = 1380 − 605 = 775 VAR, so C = Q_C/(ωV²) = 775/(314.16 × 230²) = 46.6 µF.
chapters.trap: Using peak values in VI instead of RMS, and adding apparent powers arithmetically — 100 VA at 0.6 pf plus 100 VA at 0.8 pf is not 200 VA.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for RMS, 3.3 for the impedance angle, 3.4 for finding V and I.
chapters.leave: Three-phase power to 3.6 and 3.7; AC maximum power transfer to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Three equal sinusoids 120° apart deliver the same total power at every instant and cancel in the neutral, so a balanced system collapses to one phase — and an unbalanced one does not.
chapters.depth: Phase sequence, phase voltage V_ph and line voltage V_L, star (wye) and delta loads. For star: V_L = √3 V_ph and I_L = I_ph. For delta: V_L = V_ph and I_L = √3 I_ph; in both cases the line quantity leads or lags by 30°. Balanced star and delta loads solved by a per-phase equivalent, with total P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ. Neutral current is zero when balanced; when the load is unbalanced the neutral point shifts and you solve each phase against its own impedance, then add the phase currents phasor-wise to get the neutral current. Unbalanced three-wire delta by mesh currents. Name symmetrical components as the general method and leave it.

figure.aria: A decision flow: a three-phase source is tested for balance; a balanced load goes to one per-phase circuit and then total power, an unbalanced load goes to a neutral-shift solution with unequal phase currents.

chapters.example: A balanced star-connected load of Z = 10 + j6 Ω per phase is connected to a 400 V, 50 Hz three-phase supply. Find the phase current, line current, total power and neutral current. V_ph = 400/√3 = 230.9 V. |Z| = √(100 + 36) = 11.66 Ω, so I_ph = 230.9/11.66 = 19.8 A, and in star I_L = I_ph = 19.8 A. φ = tan⁻¹(0.6) = 31.0°, cos φ = 0.857 lagging. Total P = 3 × 230.9 × 19.8 × 0.857 = 11.76 kW, which also equals √3 × 400 × 19.8 × 0.857. The neutral current is zero.
chapters.trap: Putting the √3 on the wrong quantity when changing star to delta, and assuming the neutral current stays zero once the load is unbalanced.
chapters.prereq: 3.2 and 3.3 for phasors and impedance, 3.5 for single-phase power.
chapters.leave: Two-wattmeter measurement to 3.7; symmetrical components and fault studies to a power-systems course.

chapters.idea: Two wattmeters placed in any two lines of a three-wire system give total power as W₁ + W₂ and the power-factor angle from their difference, for balanced or unbalanced loads.
chapters.depth: Connection: current coils in lines R and Y, voltage coils from R to B and from Y to B. For a balanced load W₁ = V_L I_L cos(30° + φ) and W₂ = V_L I_L cos(30° − φ). Then P = W₁ + W₂, Q = √3(W₁ − W₂) in VAR, tan φ = √3(W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂), and pf = cos φ. At φ = 60° (pf 0.5) one meter reads zero; below 0.5 pf one reading is negative and its voltage-coil terminals must be swapped to read it. Prove the two formulas for the balanced case in a few lines and state that the sum W₁ + W₂ gives total power even for an unbalanced load. Mention in one line the single-wattmeter and three-wattmeter alternatives.

figure.aria: Two wattmeter readings plotted against the load angle: at zero degrees they are equal, at 60 degrees the first falls to zero, and beyond 60 degrees it turns negative while their sum keeps falling smoothly.

chapters.example: Two wattmeters in a balanced three-phase circuit read W₁ = 5.5 kW and W₂ = 2.5 kW. Find the total power, the power factor and the reactive power. P = 5.5 + 2.5 = 8 kW. tan φ = √3(5.5 − 2.5)/(5.5 + 2.5) = 1.732 × 3/8 = 0.6495, so φ = 33.0° and pf = cos 33.0° = 0.839 lagging. Q = √3(W₁ − W₂) = 1.732 × 3 = 5.20 kVAR. Check: S = 8/0.839 = 9.54 kVA and √(9.54² − 8²) = 5.20 kVAR.
chapters.trap: Dropping the √3 in tan φ = √3(W₁ − W₂)/(W₁ + W₂), and calling a load capacitive just because one reading went negative — a negative reading only says the power factor is below 0.5.
chapters.prereq: 3.5 for complex power and power factor, 3.6 for three-phase quantities.
chapters.leave: Instrument transformers, meter construction and calibration to a measurements course; full unbalanced proofs to a power-systems course.

chapters.idea: A periodic non-sinusoidal wave is a DC term plus harmonics, so each harmonic is its own AC problem and the results combine by root-sum-square, not by simple addition.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter, so keep it short. The trigonometric Fourier series a₀/2 + Σ(aₙ cos nωt + bₙ sin nωt) with its amplitude-phase form using cₙ and φₙ. Symmetry shortcuts in one line each: even functions give cosine terms only, odd functions give sine terms only, half-wave symmetry keeps odd harmonics only. RMS of a distorted wave as the root of the sum of squared harmonic RMS values, and average power P = V₀I₀ + Σ Vₙ Iₙ cos φₙ, because cross-frequency products average to zero. Form factor of a distorted wave. THD = √(Σ Vₙ² for n ≥ 2)/V₁, quoted as a fraction or a percentage. Mention that filters decide which harmonics survive. Avoid transform theory — that belongs elsewhere.

figure.aria: A square wave approached by its Fourier partial sums: one sine term, then the fundamental plus the third harmonic, then the sum up to the seventh harmonic, each curve squarer than the last.

chapters.example: A voltage v(t) = 100 sin(314t) + 30 sin(942t + 30°) V is applied to a circuit. Find its RMS value and the THD. The 942 rad/s term is exactly the third harmonic of 314 rad/s. Fundamental RMS = 100/√2 = 70.7 V, third harmonic RMS = 30/√2 = 21.2 V. Total RMS = √(70.7² + 21.2²) = √(5000 + 450) = 73.8 V. THD = 21.2/70.7 = 0.30, that is 30 %.
chapters.trap: Adding harmonic RMS values directly (70.7 + 21.2 = 91.9 V is wrong), and expecting a third-harmonic current to produce average power with a fundamental voltage.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 for RMS, 3.2 for phasors, 3.5 for average power.
chapters.leave: Frequency response, filters and cut-off frequencies to Unit 4; Fourier and Laplace transform methods to Unit 5.
